text:
FORT LEAVENWORTH, Kansas — Fort Leavenworth community members visited Munson Army Health Center Aug. 12 for “Operation Know Your MTF,” an open house designed to connect service members, military families and retirees with healthcare, readiness and support services.

Attendees came for a variety of services including Military Treatment Facility enrollment information, TRICARE and EFMP support, and special walk-in Individual Medical Readiness screening hours for service members starting a rigorous academic year at the U.S. Army Command and General Staff College,

“Our goal was to give our beneficiaries direct access to the people who can help them navigate their healthcare,” said Col. Jolanda L.J. Walker, director of Munson Army Health Center. “Scheduling the open house during a staff training afternoon allowed us to welcome the community while minimizing the impact on patient care. Team members supporting the event connected beneficiaries with services, while other staff continued their scheduled training.”

During the two-hour event, service members completed MEDPROS vision and/or hearing, lab, and immunization requirements. The Fort Leavenworth Armed Forces Wellness Center representatives welcomed beneficiaries to their new location within Munson and booked Bod Pod and other wellness appointments.

Others obtained documentation of previously completed school and sports physicals from Medical Records, enabling new families to move forward with school requirements at their new duty station. In Primary Care staff assisted families with EFMP-related questions and processes and families were able to meet Munson’s new pediatrician Dr. Lucy Lot.

“Holding the event the afternoon after the Command and General Staff College Spouse Night allowed newly arrived families to receive follow-on assistance,” said Walker.

Representatives from Munson’s clinical, readiness and support services were positioned throughout the health center. A self-guided mission map helped visitors choose the programs most relevant to them while becoming more familiar with the facility.

Public Health and the laboratory experienced particularly high visitor traffic. Rehabilitation and Physical Therapy personnel connected patients with care, while approximately 40 attendees participated in the clinic’s popular grip-strength challenge.

Smith Dental Clinic, which serves active duty, also provided information about dental care for family members through the TRICARE Dental Program. A TriWest representative was also available to assist beneficiaries and the pharmacy remained open for routine prescription pickup throughout the event.

The open house also strengthened coordination with installation and community partners like Army Community Service, Family Advocacy Program, and Fort Leavenworth Department of Emergency Service. The installation’s new emergency medical services contract representative and EMS team members connected with the health center’s Operations team to discuss future collaboration, including Basic Life Support and CPR sustainment programs. The EMS team also educated community members on accessing 911 from post. Calls are routed through a regional dispatch so callers must specify they’re located on post.

Overall, the open house gave beneficiaries a single location to address healthcare, readiness and administrative needs while becoming better acquainted with their military treatment facility.

text:
Advisors including former Defense Health Agency Director Vice Admiral Dr. Raquel C. Bono, and retired four-star Generals Paul E. Funk II and Michael X. Garrett will help guide Rebound's efforts to deliver specialty trauma treatment to Active Military and Veterans

Rebound Health, a Noto company and the only national virtual specialty therapy provider for PTSD, today announced that a number of senior military and industry leaders have joined its advisory board to expand trauma care for Active Military and Veterans. The advisors bring decades of experience in military command, medicine, and Veteran care.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260820089212/en/

"At Noto, our mission is to end the mental health crisis by delivering world-class specialty therapy to every population that needs it," said Stephen Smith, Co-Founder and CEO of Noto and NOCD. "Active military and Veterans with PTS are among the communities hit hardest by this crisis. That's why we're honored to partner with Dr. Bono, General Funk, General Garrett, Dr. Shulkin, General LeMaster, Bob Jansen and Al Reicheg — and I'm confident we can make a major difference together, given what we've proven by scaling NOCD on the Noto platform, the impact these leaders have had in supporting our nation's military, and the incredible outcomes Rebound has already produced for trauma survivors.”

Vice Admiral Dr. Raquel C. Bono (retired), former Director of the Defense Health Agency, oversaw health care for millions of active-duty personnel, retirees, and their families. General Paul E. Funk II (retired) last served as Commander of the U.S. Army Training and Doctrine Command (TRADOC) and previously led a 72-nation coalition against ISIS as Commander of Combined Joint Task Force–Operation Inherent Resolve. General Michael X. Garrett (retired) is the former Commanding General of the U.S. Army Forces Command, the Army’s largest command. They are joined by Dr. David Shulkin, the Ninth Secretary of the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs; Major General Dennis LeMaster (retired), former Commanding General of the U.S. Army Medical Center of Excellence; and former senior pharmaceutical executives Bob Jansen, CEO of Zensights, and Al Reicheg, CEO of Sea Change Healthcare Consulting. Collectively, the group spent their careers responsible for the health, care, and readiness of millions of Service Members and their families.

What drew them to Rebound is the company's answer to a problem they know intimately: high-quality PTSD treatment is hard to reach for the people who need it most. Active Duty Service Members often can't leave base to get care. Veterans in rural areas may be hours from a specialist. Rebound's model removes that barrier—delivering specialty trauma treatment virtually, in all 50 states, so treatment reaches the Member rather than requiring the Member to travel to a specialty clinic. Moreover, Rebound is owned by Noto and scaled on its platform, the same infrastructure used to effectively scale NOCD for OCD and Related Disorders.

"The infrastructure the NOCD team built is what lets us deliver the best PTSD treatment there is at national scale, at the clinical standard it demands—when we treat someone, we do it the right way," said Raeva Kumar, CEO and co-founder of Rebound. "Millions of Service Members and Veterans are suffering today, and they can't wait for care that works. Those of us who have received effective treatment have a responsibility to the people still waiting in silence. These leaders have spent their careers getting care to this community, and there's a great deal we intend to learn from them."

Vice Admiral Dr. Raquel C. Bono, who joins the advisory board, said, “We are honored to continue to support those who have served and continue to serve our nation by ensuring that they have access to the highest standard of evidence-based PTS treatment. Rebound combines a network of exceptional trauma specialists with technology that helps people stay engaged in treatment when a provider isn’t available, no matter where they live. That's the future of trauma care."

Rebound identifies and engages Members with PTSD through content, community, and technology, then connects them to face-to-face care with full-time, Rebound therapists who are carefully selected and rigorously trained in Prolonged Exposure therapy—the gold-standard treatment for PTSD. Each Rebound Therapist then must test into the Rebound Network. Care includes continuous between-session support, creating a true 24/7/365 treatment model rather than a weekly appointment in isolation. The company is in-network with most major insurers and operates as a sister brand to NOCD on the Noto platform.

The model is delivering results. On average, Members receive an average of 13 sessions of PE—a full course of treatment—with 67% achieving clinically meaningful improvement in PTSD symptoms, defined as a ≥10-point reduction on the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5), one of the most widely used measures of PTSD symptom severity.

"We know how to treat PTSD. The challenge is delivering those outcomes consistently, at scale, without compromising quality," said Dr. Erin Berenz, co-founder and Chief Clinical Officer of Rebound. "That's exactly the challenge NOCD has solved for OCD, and I’m thrilled to expand that model to Rebound and scale access to evidence-based PTSD treatment without sacrificing clinical excellence. We're proud of the progress we've made so far, and having these advisors help shape what comes next is an extraordinary opportunity for Rebound and for the Service Members and Veterans we're here to serve."

The advisors will work with Noto and Rebound's clinical and operating leadership to deepen the company's ability to serve Active Duty, Veteran, and military-family populations.

Rebound is a virtual specialty therapy company treating PTSD and related conditions, operating in all 50 states and in-network with most major insurers. Rebound engages members through content, community, and technology, then connects them to face-to-face care with full-time, in-house clinicians carefully selected and rigorously trained in Prolonged Exposure therapy, with continuous 24/7/365 between-session support. Rebound was acquired by Noto in 2025 and operates under the Noto parent company as a sister brand to NOCD, focused on trauma and PTSD recovery. Learn more at hellorebound.com.

Noto is an AI-enabled platform that’s transforming specialty therapy to end the mental health crisis, by scaling virtual specialties for complex psychiatric and behavioral conditions: NOCD for OCD and, most recently, Rebound for PTSD, with the expectation of more to come.

Our Mission

To unite the best of public service and private enterprise through a premier strategic network advancing the health, well-being, and economic security of the people who support, serve, and have served our nation.

text:
Researchers in the School of Dental Medicine received the 2026 Military Health System Research Symposium Award for Excellence, Outstanding Research Accomplishment Award for their work in developing a multifunctional biomaterial platform for combat casualty care—uniting hemorrhage control, tissue regeneration, and pain management within a single, adaptable platform.

Dr. Ivo Kalajzic, professor of regenerative medicine and skeletal development, and Dr. Ali Tamayol, professor of biomedical engineering, lead a team of researchers from UConn Health with Dr. Sangamesh Kumbar from University of Nebraska Medical Center on this award-wining project.

“This well-deserved recognition demonstrates the highly innovative and clinically relevant work being done by our researchers” says Rajesh V. Lalla, DDS, PhD, Associate Dean for Research at the UConn School of Dental Medicine. “The notable success of this multidisciplinary team, including trainees and faculty at various career stages, also speaks to the excellent scientific and educational environment at UConn Health.”

Complex combat-related injuries frequently involve simultaneous damage to multiple tissue types, including bone, muscle, and skin, and are often compounded by uncontrolled hemorrhage and prolonged pain. Current treatment strategies typically address these challenges in isolation, requiring multiple interventions that increase logistical burden and delay recovery. There remains a critical need for integrated, field-deployable solutions capable of stabilizing acute injuries while promoting coordinated, long-term tissue regeneration.

The team of researchers engineered rapidly deployable, tissue-specific foams that enable immediate hemorrhage control while promoting bone and muscle regeneration. Using a murine bone-muscle defect model, which captures the biological interplay between tissues normally absent in traditional single-tissue studies, the researchers demonstrated that compartment-specific therapeutic strategies are more effective than uniform treatment approaches. The tissue-specific scaffolds are tailored to the distinct regenerative requirements of both bone and tissue. The materials are also highly adaptable, capable of injection, printing, or spray-based delivery, and conform to irregular wound geometries and adhere to wet tissue surfaces without external triggers.

A key advancement of innovation included the discovery that the materials that make up the foams not only support bone growth, but also exhibit intrinsic hemostatic properties, significantly accelerating clot formation and stabilizing bleeding at the wound site. This finding enabled the extension of the platform to acute hemorrhage control, allowing immediate injury stabilization prior to regenerative intervention, without introducing additional materials or complexity.

The impact of this work lies in its ability to address multiple unmet clinical needs simultaneously and represents a significant step towards adaptable, field-ready solutions for improving warfighter outcomes.

The funding for this research is supported by two United States Department of War grants, HT9425-24-1-0944 and HT9425-25-1-0772

text:
YOKOTA AIR BASE, Japan — The urgent care clinic at this airlift hub in western Tokyo will move into larger quarters this weekend, giving it more room for patients and treatment but representing a change separate from the Pentagon’s recent push to improve emergency care at U.S. bases in Japan.

The locally driven relocation took more than a year to plan, Defense Health Agency spokesman Peter Graves said by email Wednesday.

The 374th Medical Group announced the move in an Aug. 4 Facebook post and said the clinic will close from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday while its staff and equipment are relocated.

The new space will provide a larger waiting area, more treatment areas and additional storage, Graves said. Full 911 capabilities will remain available during the move.

The clinic’s 30-person urgent care team and its equipment will swap locations with the hospital’s five-person orthopedic surgery clinic, 374th Airlift Wing spokesman Capt. Steve Garrett said in an Aug. 11 email.

The “current location was not originally designed for Urgent Care operations, and we have an opportunity to relocate to a more optimal and larger space,” he wrote.

The move comes as the Pentagon has been strengthening emergency medical capabilities at U.S. installations across Japan. The Defense Department reported last year that it spent $10.8 million on improvements to on-base medical facilities in the country.

Changes outlined in a 2025 report to a congressional defense committee included nine new active-duty paramedic billets at Yokota, Kadena and Misawa air bases, rotations of emergency physicians to Yokota and Misawa and a phased increase in trauma nurses.

The personnel increases are intended to bolster trauma support and emergency transport capabilities at U.S. military bases in Japan, according to the report.

“Civilian nurses completed additional trauma training to provide stabilization during emergent, life-threatening events, to enhance emergency response,” the report said.

The Pentagon also reported purchasing new medical equipment for facilities in Japan, including ultrasound and MRI machines at naval hospitals on Okinawa and at Yokosuka Naval Base and a washer sterilizer at Yokota.

“The procurement of additional supplies and medical equipment will expand services offered and assignment of additional medical personnel will further contribute to emergency medical operations and reduce risks associated with patient stabilization,” the report said.

Graves stressed that Yokota’s urgent care relocation is a “proactive, scheduled workflow optimization” and is not connected to previous emergency-care incidents.

The deaths of two civilian Defense Department employees treated at Yokota in 2021 and 2023 prompted complaints about emergency medical care available to Americans at the base and their access to Japanese hospitals.

Andrew Hakun, who worked for the Department of Defense Special Representative in Japan, suffered a heart attack at his Yokota home in February 2021.

After he was taken to the urgent care clinic, staff contacted more than 10 hospitals before finding one in Hachioji, about 7 miles from the base, that would accept him, according to his medical records. Hakun had already suffered brain damage and died two days later in a central Tokyo hospital.

In 2023, then-Yokota spokesman 1st Lt. Danny Rangel said military urgent care centers provide stabilizing care but transfer higher-level cases to Japanese facilities.

Robert Hawthorne, chief of American Forces Network Pacific’s technical services division, died at the clinic after suffering a heart attack in February 2023.

His wife, Kim Hawthorne, blamed the clinic’s inability to provide lifesaving treatment in serious health emergencies and a lack of guaranteed care at Japanese facilities for U.S. military personnel for contributing to her husband’s death.

text:
Preparing professionals to detect, assess, and manage deliberate biothreat events and laboratory biosafety incidents requires more than theoretical knowledge — it demands practiced decision-making under pressure, across disciplines and sectors. A two-day tabletop simulation exercise designed to build precisely that capacity is scheduled for August 2026 in Singapore.

The Biosecurity Simulation Exercise (BSX 2026), organized by the Asia Centre for Health Security, will take place on 27–28 August 2026 at the Grand Copthorne Waterfront Hotel, Singapore. The exercise employs lectures, guided discussions, and structured, scenario-driven simulations to immerse participants in realistic, high-consequence biological incidents that unfold under conditions of incomplete information.

The exercise is designed around three core objectives: strengthening surveillance, preparedness, and response capabilities for laboratory biosafety and biosecurity (LBB) incidents and deliberate biothreat events (DBE); enhancing inter-sectoral and inter-disciplinary coordination and decision-making through team-based problem-solving; and reviewing the legal, policy, and security dimensions relevant to public health responses to such incidents. Working in collaborative teams, participants will address challenges spanning surveillance, diagnostics, public health response, security assessment, and risk communication.

The event is intended for professionals whose work intersects with laboratory biosafety and biosecurity or with bioterrorism preparedness and response. Target attendees include practitioners from public health, clinical medicine, laboratory sciences, policy, defence, and law enforcement. Proficiency in written and spoken English is required for full participation.

For public health security and biosecurity professionals, BSX 2026 offers a structured opportunity to stress-test response frameworks and inter-agency coordination in a consequence-free environment. The exercise’s explicitly inter-sectoral design — bridging public health, security, and policy communities — reflects the operational realities of managing high-consequence biological events, where effective response depends on coordination across institutions and disciplines that do not routinely work together.

The full programme has not yet been released. Interested participants are encouraged to monitor the event page for updates on sessions, speakers, and registration details.

Are you curious about how TRICARE, Medicare, and Social Security work together?

Many service members and their families don’t realize that Social Security taxes deducted from each paycheck help build a foundation for future financial security. You’ve been paying into Social Security, so keeping tabs on your information is key.

Signing up for Medicare Part A and Part B is required to get TRICARE For Life coverage. And the Social Security Administration handles enrollment for Medicare.

By setting up a my Social Security account, you can see what you’ve earned, and how it all fits together. You don’t have to wait until retirement or age 65 to start managing your benefits. Setting up an account early in your military journey helps you:

Track earned credits

Verify your military earnings

Plan for your family's future

Let’s take a closer look at the benefits.

What are my Social Security benefits?

Retirement benefits: Your retirement benefit amount is based on your 35 highest earning years. This includes your military earnings covered by Social Security taxes. You may choose to begin receiving retirement benefits early as age 62. Or delay benefits for a higher monthly amount.

Disability benefits: Social Security Disability Insurance may be available if you have a qualifying medical condition that prevents you from working and you meet work credit requirements. SSDI is separate from VA disability compensation. Some veterans may qualify for both.

Survivor benefits: Are you an eligible spouse, child, or other family member? You may qualify for survivor benefits based on a worker’s earnings record. These benefits are separate from military survivor programs.

Medicare and TRICARE For Life: Social Security taxes also help fund Medicare. Most people become eligible for Medicare at age 65. You need to sign up for Medicare Part A and Part B to get and keep TFL coverage. You must pay Medicare Part B premiums.

How can a my Social Security account help me?

A personal my Social Security account gives you secure access to important Social Security information and online services. Creating an account is free. It can be done with your existing Login.gov or ID.me credentials.

Update your mailing address and phone number

View your benefit amount and information

text:
Researchers shared new findings on biosurveillance, antimicrobial resistance, and infectious disease countermeasures at the 2026 Military Health System Research Symposium, held August 3-6 in Florida. Among more than 3,700 attendees, dozens of research teams presented work with direct relevance to biosecurity and public health preparedness, from wastewater surveillance systems tracking drug resistant bacteria in real time to a new vaccine candidate targeting one of the most difficult to treat pathogens in modern medicine.

Biosurveillance Systems Aim to Catch Outbreaks Earlier

Several studies focused on turning biosurveillance data into something decision makers can actually act on. In a poster presentation, MIT Lincoln Laboratory researchers outlined a framework for evaluating whether biodetection systems produce genuinely useful information, not just data. Their analysis found that actionability depends on more than speed. It also requires confidence in results that matches the stakes of the decision being made. A companion poster from the same team described a modeling framework that simulates how early warning from biosurveillance might change outcomes during an infectious disease outbreak, whether from an intentional release or a naturally occurring pathogen such as plague or a novel respiratory virus. The models suggest that even modest gains in early information can meaningfully change how much combat power and medical capacity an outbreak ultimately costs.

That push toward real-time detection is already showing up in the field. The Defense Centers for Public Health in Aberdeen, Maryland, took the podium Tuesday afternoon as part of a session on Global Health Engagement to describe a wastewater surveillance dashboard built for the Indo-Pacific Command that tracks 12 viral pathogens weekly across multiple installations, giving decision makers early warning before clinic visits start to climb. Researchers at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center presented data pairing wastewater genomic sequencing with hospital antibiotic resistance data. Their system detected resistance genes circulating in the hospital population before they showed up in traditional clinical testing, and the team estimates the approach could save one to two weeks of manual work each year while catching emerging resistance trends sooner.

In Southeast Asia, WRAIR’s Armed Forces Research Institute of Medical Sciences has spent the past three years running real time molecular surveillance during major regional military exercises, testing hundreds of samples from service members with respiratory or diarrheal illness within 48 hours. That work turned up a notable and unexpected pattern: most respiratory viruses detected during these exercises appeared to originate in the United States and continue spreading among personnel during the event, rather than being picked up locally. The same program also confirmed high rates of ciprofloxacin resistance among diarrheal pathogens, while azithromycin remained largely effective, information that directly shapes field treatment guidance.

Platform Technologies Target Select Agents and Biothreat Pathogens

A session titled “Platform Technologies: Revolutionizing Infectious Disease Countermeasures for the Military,” moderated by Appavu Sundaram and John Dye, brought podium visibility to a cluster of research aimed at a shared problem: building medical countermeasures fast enough to matter against a threat agent that has not yet been identified.

Qoolabs Inc. opened the session with a rapid antibody discovery platform built around the “100-Day Mission,” a goal of producing fieldable diagnostics and prophylactic antibodies within 100 days of identifying a new viral threat. The company’s platform uses AI integrated single cell antibody screening to identify high affinity candidate antibodies in under eight weeks, with humanization completed in two additional weeks. In presented results, lead antibodies reached picomolar affinity within 50 days, and the team is currently developing rapid diagnostic tests for Ebola and Marburg virus under a BARDA contract, with a manufacturing partner capable of producing 80 million lateral flow tests annually.

Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory presented a complementary delivery platform built around nanolipoprotein particles, engineered nanoscale carriers modeled on the structure of high-density lipoproteins that can co-deliver vaccine antigens and adjuvants in a single formulation. Researchers demonstrated successful conjugation of antigens from three Tier 1 select agents, Yersinia pestis, Francisella tularensis, and Burkholderia pseudomallei, the bacteria responsible for plague, tularemia, and melioidosis. Multi-pathogen formulations protected rodents in aerosol challenge models as effectively as single-pathogen versions, a result with direct relevance to scenarios involving simultaneous or unknown biological exposures.

A third team presented work on transchromosomic bovines, cattle genetically modified to produce fully human polyclonal antibodies rather than bovine antibodies. The platform has already generated antibody candidates against Ebola, MERS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2, influenza, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus, Zika, pneumonic plague, anthrax, and dengue, spanning both naturally occurring and potential biowarfare threats. Three products derived from the platform have reached human clinical trials, including one that completed Phase 2 and Phase 3 testing under the federal ACTIV-2 program during the COVID-19 pandemic. Because the antibodies target multiple epitopes simultaneously, the developers argue the approach is more resistant to viral escape through mutation than single target monoclonal antibody treatments, and can scale to more than 300 grams of human immunoglobulin per animal per month.

That podium session complemented poster work on countermeasures against two other named biothreat agents. BARDA shared interim results from a clinical trial testing whether a lower dose of the anthrax vaccine CYFENDUS could maintain effectiveness while extending the number of available doses during a public health emergency, finding that half doses performed comparably to full doses in triggering an immune response. And Tonix Pharmaceutical presented data on a new orthopoxvirus vaccine platform that proved substantially more attenuated than older smallpox vaccine strains while still protecting animals against lethal mpox challenge, including the more severe clade I strain, suggesting a path toward safer next generation vaccines against mpox and related viruses.

Underpinning much of this work is an institutional effort to move promising prototypes out of the laboratory faster. The Defense Threat Reduction Agency’s Joint Science and Technology Office described its Laboratory Analysis and Clinical Evaluation program, which independently validates diagnostic prototypes for chemical and biological threats and has transitioned four diagnostic capabilities into operational use over the past three years, with field testing conducted during exercises such as Salaknib 26.

Drug Resistant Infections Present a Growing Threat in Conflict Zones and Beyond

Antimicrobial resistance emerged as a recurring theme across multiple research abstracts, with some of the most sobering data coming out of the war in Ukraine. Researchers with WRAIR Europe-Middle East characterized bacterial isolates collected from wounded patients and found a troubling pattern: while resistant organisms were relatively rare in wounds shortly after injury, hospitals in Kharkiv yielded hundreds of multidrug resistant isolates that were nearly genetically identical to strains circulating before the conflict began, pointing to ongoing transmission within hospital walls rather than contamination on the battlefield. The vast majority of Acinetobacter baumannii isolates tested were resistant to carbapenems, a last line antibiotic class, and researchers found several concerning strains carrying both resistance and virulence genes.

Elsewhere, a Defense Centers for Public Health team analyzed nearly a million bacterial isolates collected from military health system patients between 2014 and 2024, tracking resistance patterns in seven pathogens the World Health Organization and CDC consider priority threats. The data show a decline in total isolates collected over the decade, though the researchers caution this may partly reflect changes in where military patients are tested rather than a true drop in infections. Separately, data presented on surveillance at Tripler and Madigan Army Medical Centers found extremely high rates of resistance markers in Neisseria gonorrhoeae, with genetic signs of resistance to macrolide antibiotics present in the vast majority of isolates tested, a finding researchers linked to the transient nature of military populations and regional travel patterns across the Pacific.

On the countermeasure side, a team from Biological Mimetics reported early success with what would be the first vaccine candidate against Acinetobacter baumannii, a bacterium nicknamed Iraqi-bacter for its association with combat wound infections and one that health agencies have flagged as an urgent threat due to widespread carbapenem resistance. In mouse models, the vaccine protected 90 percent of animals from a lethal lung infection.

Taken together, the research shared at this year’s symposium, whether from the podium or the poster hall, reflects a military health enterprise increasingly focused on catching threats earlier and closing gaps in treatment options for pathogens that no longer respond reliably to existing drugs, priorities that extend well beyond the battlefield to public health readiness more broadly.

How Does TRICARE Work?

TRICARE is the U.S. military’s health care program for eligible service members, retirees, and their families. Established in 1993 to replace the former CHAMPUS program, TRICARE combines military hospitals and clinics with civilian healthcare providers. Eligibility generally includes active-duty service members, National Guard and Reserve members, retirees, eligible spouses and children, survivors, and certain other qualified family members, with eligibility based on military status and registration in DEERS. People without an eligible military affiliation generally cannot enroll in TRICARE. For rehab treatment, TRICARE may cover medically necessary substance use disorder services such as detox, inpatient and residential rehab, PHP, IOP, medication-assisted treatment, and opioid treatment programs. Residential treatment requires pre-authorization, and other services may have specific referral or authorization requirements. Individuals also cannot necessarily choose any rehab facility; the facility must meet TRICARE requirements, and using an authorized or network provider can help reduce out-of-pocket costs.

What Addictions Does TRICARE Cover in Texas?

TRICARE may cover treatment for a range of substance use disorders in Texas, including alcohol addiction, opioid addiction, heroin addiction, fentanyl addiction, prescription drug addiction, cocaine addiction, methamphetamine addiction, benzodiazepine addiction, marijuana or cannabis addiction, and tobacco or nicotine dependence. TRICARE also covers treatment for substance use involving other illicit or misused drugs when care is medically or psychologically necessary.

What Addiction Treatments & Therapies Does TRICARE Cover in Texas?

TRICARE in Texas generally covers a variety of addiction treatments and therapies. Coverage is designed to support recovery through different levels of care tailored to the severity of the substance use disorder and the member’s individual needs. The following are common addiction treatments that may be covered:

Medical Detox: Short-term supervised withdrawal management, typically 3 to 7 days, depending on the substance and severity of withdrawal.

Inpatient Rehab: 24/7 hospital-based or residential care for stabilization and intensive therapy, generally 7 to 30 days.

Residential Treatment: Structured, live-in programs offering comprehensive therapy and support, usually 30 to 90 days.

Partial Hospitalization Program (PHP): Day treatment programs providing intensive therapy while allowing patients to return home in the evenings, often 4 to 6 hours per day for several weeks.

Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP): Flexible programs with 9 to 20 hours per week over 4 to 12 weeks, allowing patients to maintain daily responsibilities while receiving therapy.

Outpatient Treatment: Regular therapy sessions for ongoing support and relapse prevention, typically 1 to 2 sessions per week for several months.

Specific addiction treatment therapies TRICARE covers may include:

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT): Helps patients recognize and change negative thought patterns and behaviors that contribute to substance use. CBT often includes coping skills, relapse prevention strategies, and problem-solving exercises tailored to addiction triggers.

Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR): A trauma-focused therapy that helps patients process past traumatic experiences, reduce emotional distress, and address trauma-related triggers that can lead to substance use relapse.

Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT): Focuses on emotional regulation, distress tolerance, mindfulness, and interpersonal effectiveness. DBT is especially helpful for individuals with high emotional reactivity or co-occurring borderline personality traits.

Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT): Teaches patients to identify and challenge irrational beliefs or cognitive distortions that contribute to addictive behaviors, promoting healthier decision-making and self-control.

Dual Diagnosis Programs: Integrated treatment for co-occurring mental health disorders such as depression, anxiety, PTSD, or bipolar disorder alongside substance use disorders. Treating both conditions simultaneously improves recovery outcomes and reduces relapse risk.

12-Step Programs: Peer-supported programs like Alcoholics Anonymous or Narcotics Anonymous that provide structure, accountability, and a community-based approach to long-term recovery through sponsorship and step work.

SMART Recovery: A science-based approach to addiction recovery that focuses on self-empowerment, goal setting, motivation, and cognitive-behavioral techniques rather than spirituality or peer-led steps.

Holistic Therapies: Complementary approaches such as yoga, meditation, acupuncture, art therapy, or nutrition counseling that address physical, emotional, and spiritual well-being to support overall recovery.

Family Therapy: Involves family members in treatment to improve communication, repair relationships, and build a supportive home environment that encourages sustained recovery.

Group Therapy: Provides peer support and shared learning experiences, allowing patients to discuss challenges, gain accountability, and practice interpersonal skills in a structured setting.

Individual Therapy: One-on-one sessions with a licensed therapist tailored to the patient’s unique needs, focusing on personal triggers, coping strategies, and treatment goals.

Specific Tracks: Specialized programs designed for particular populations, such as veterans, professionals, LGBTQ+ individuals, or young adults. These tracks offer tailored therapy approaches, peer communities, and culturally competent care to address unique challenges and life experiences.

Does TRICARE Cover Addiction Medications?

Yes, TRICARE may cover medications used to treat substance use disorders when they are medically necessary and meet TRICARE’s coverage requirements. Common medications used in addiction treatment include buprenorphine (such as Suboxone) and methadone for opioid use disorder, which can reduce cravings and withdrawal symptoms, as well as naltrexone, which can help reduce alcohol cravings and prevent opioid effects. TRICARE specifically covers medication-assisted treatment (MAT), which combines medication with counseling or other behavioral health services. MAT may be provided through opioid treatment programs or office-based opioid treatment, including by qualified providers authorized to prescribe buprenorphine. Prescription coverage depends on the TRICARE Formulary, and some medications may require prior authorization or other requirements.

Does TRICARE Cover Dual Diagnosis Treatment in Texas?

Yes, TRICARE may cover dual diagnosis treatment in Texas when care is medically or psychologically necessary for both a substance use disorder and a co-occurring mental health condition. This can be especially important for veterans and military families, as experiences such as combat, trauma, and other stressful events can contribute to conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, anxiety, and substance use disorders. Treating both conditions together can help address the underlying causes of addiction, manage mental health symptoms, and support a more lasting recovery.

How Long Will TRICARE Cover Rehab in Texas?

TRICARE coverage for rehab in Texas varies by plan and level of care, but typical treatment ranges may include medical detox: 3–7 days, residential rehab: 30–90 days, partial hospitalization (PHP): 2–6 weeks, and intensive outpatient (IOP): 4–12 weeks. Longer stays may be approved when medically necessary and supported by the individual’s treatment needs and insurance benefits.

Benefits of Using Insurance for Rehab

Lower or No Out-of-Pocket Costs: Insurance can cover most or all of rehab expenses, reducing financial barriers or even making treatment free for the member.

Access to Accredited In-Network Facilities: Members can use licensed and reputable rehab centers without paying full self-pay rates.

Coverage for Multiple Levels of Care: Detox, inpatient, residential, partial hospitalization, outpatient, and intensive outpatient programs are often included.

Evidence-Based Therapies Covered: Therapies like CBT, DBT, EMDR, REBT, and medication-assisted treatment are included, reducing additional therapy costs.

Dual Diagnosis Support: Integrated treatment for mental health and substance use disorders is covered, avoiding separate payments for each condition.

Aftercare and Relapse Prevention: Ongoing therapy, support groups, and follow-up care may be included at little or no cost.

Personalized Treatment Planning: Insurance often ensures assessments and care plans are provided without extra fees.

Access to Holistic and Complementary Services: Some plans cover wellness-focused services like yoga, meditation, art therapy, or acupuncture, reducing the need to pay out-of-pocket.

Care Coordination and Advocacy: Insurance helps manage prior authorization and documentation, preventing unexpected bills.

Encourages Early Intervention: Coverage can allow members to seek treatment quickly, avoiding costly medical complications later.

Confidentiality Protections: Insurance ensures records are handled according to federal privacy laws at no extra cost to the patient.

How Much Does Rehab Cost Without Insurance in Texas?

Without insurance, the cost of rehab in Texas can vary widely depending on the level of care, length of stay, location, amenities, and type of program. Medical detox typically ranges from $2,500 to $10,000 for a short medically supervised withdrawal period. Inpatient or residential rehab programs generally cost between $12,000 and $30,000 per month, with 60‑ to 90‑day stays often totaling $25,000 to $50,000 or more. Partial hospitalization programs (PHP) usually range from $300 to $600 per day, while intensive outpatient programs (IOP) cost around $250 to $450 per day, with multi‑week programs totaling several thousand dollars. Standard outpatient treatment, including regular counseling and therapy over three to four months, typically costs $3,000 to $10,000 or more.

Several variables impact the total cost of rehab. Higher levels of care like inpatient or residential treatment are more expensive than outpatient care. Longer stays increase costs, and luxury facilities with private rooms, specialized therapies, or premium services often charge more. The types of therapies and support services offered, the location of the facility, and the credentials of staff, including access to medical doctors or psychiatric specialists, also affect pricing. Actual costs vary by facility and the patient’s specific treatment needs, so contacting rehab centers directly is recommended for precise estimates.

What Won’t TRICARE Cover for Addiction Treatment in Texas?

TRICARE generally does not cover addiction treatment services that are not medically or psychologically necessary, unproven, or provided by an unauthorized provider. Specific exclusions can include aversion therapy, experimental or unproven treatments, alternative treatments, long-term care, and services that are considered primarily custodial rather than therapeutic. Certain non-clinical services and programs may also fall outside coverage. Residential substance use disorder treatment and other higher levels of care may require pre-authorization, and coverage can vary by plan and beneficiary status.

Will Addiction or Rehab Affect My Veteran Benefits?

Addiction does not automatically cause a veteran to lose VA benefits or disability compensation. However, substance use can affect certain disability claims if a condition is determined to have resulted from the veteran’s own alcohol or drug abuse or willful misconduct. At the same time, veterans may qualify for benefits related to service-connected conditions such as PTSD, depression, anxiety, or other mental health disorders, and substance use may occur alongside or be related to those conditions. Seeking treatment for addiction does not by itself mean a veteran will lose existing benefits and may provide access to additional treatment and support through the VA. Because individual circumstances can affect specific claims and benefits, veterans with concerns should speak with an accredited VA representative about their situation.

Getting treatment for drug or alcohol addiction generally does not automatically affect a veteran’s VA benefits, disability compensation, or eligibility for VA health care. Veterans’ addiction treatment records have special confidentiality protections under federal law, including 38 U.S.C. § 7332 and 42 CFR Part 2, which limit when substance use disorder information can be disclosed. Rehab treatment typically does not appear on a standard criminal background check simply because a person received treatment, and protected health information generally cannot be shared with employers or other parties without authorization or another legally permitted reason. Using TRICARE or another insurance plan for rehab will create a healthcare and insurance record for claims and payment purposes, but this is different from a public or criminal record. While treatment itself does not normally result in a loss of veteran benefits, certain employment, licensing, security-clearance, disability, or legal circumstances may involve additional considerations.

Can TRICARE Cover Rehab for a Veteran’s Spouse or Children?

Yes, TRICARE can cover drug and alcohol rehab for an eligible veteran’s spouse or children if they qualify as TRICARE beneficiaries and are registered in the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System (DEERS). Eligibility generally depends on the veteran or service member’s military status, such as being an active-duty service member, retiree, or qualifying National Guard or Reserve member, as well as the family member’s relationship and age. Spouses are generally eligible while they remain married to an eligible sponsor, while dependent children may qualify until certain age limits, with some options available for young adults who age out of regular coverage.

History & About TRICARE

TRICARE is the U.S. military health care program serving active-duty service members, National Guard and Reserve members, retirees, and eligible family members. Established in 1993, TRICARE replaced the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Uniformed Services (CHAMPUS) and initially offered TRICARE Prime, TRICARE Extra, and TRICARE Standard. Prime provided managed care, Extra gave beneficiaries access to preferred civilian providers, and Standard operated as a fee-for-service option. Over the years, TRICARE expanded to meet the needs of different military populations and locations. Today, available plans include TRICARE Prime, TRICARE Prime Remote, TRICARE Select, TRICARE For Life, TRICARE Reserve Select, TRICARE Retired Reserve, TRICARE Young Adult, overseas coverage options, and the Uniformed Services Family Health Plan. TRICARE provides coverage for preventive care, doctor visits, hospital services, prescription medications, specialty care, mental health treatment, and substance use disorder treatment. TRICARE For Life provides Medicare-wraparound coverage for eligible beneficiaries with Medicare Part A and Part B, while TRICARE Young Adult allows certain eligible unmarried adult children to purchase coverage after aging out of regular TRICARE eligibility.

HOW TO VERIFY YOUR INSURANCE COVERAGE

Dealing with health insurance companies on your own can be a hassle. You may not know what to say or what kinds of questions you need to ask to ensure your insurance provider is working in your best interest. It adds unnecessary stress to an already trying situation. That’s why Discovery Point Retreat’s admissions support includes insurance verification help. REHAB PAYMENT OPTIONS WITHOUT INSURANCE

If you are uninsured or your health insurance does not cover the cost of rehab, all hope is not lost. There are still options for you to be able to get the treatment you need for a sober future. Discovery Point Retreat accepts self-pay options including cash, debit and credit, and certified check. Other options for covering your treatment include:

text:
Army TEIS IV

The window is now open for companies to work on and turn in bids to join the potential $800 million Total Engineering and Integration Services IV contract, which opened for business in 2021.

TEIS IV covers a broad range of information systems engineering services, with an emphasis on cybersecurity and communications. A total of six companies participate as primes on this contract, which three companies won seats on in 2020 and another trio was chosen for in 2021.

Up to 10 new companies will be selected for the on-ramp, with four of those seats reserved for small businesses, the Army said in its Wednesday notice to release the final solicitation.

Bids for the on-ramp are due to the Army Information Systems Engineering Command by 6 p.m. Eastern time on Oct. 7.

Awardees compete for task orders across work areas that include planning, design, development, engineering, implementation, procurement, logistics, evaluation, test, sustainment, systems retirement and ancillary services.

The Army has obligated $160 million in task order volume to-date against TEIS IV, with Empower AI as the top recipient of the spend at 65%, according to GovTribe data.

TEIS IV’s period of performance includes an initial five-year base period, followed by a single option for five additional years.

DHA Omnibus IV

The Defense Health Agency has taken a first step in preparing to open the window for 8(a) small businesses to pursue a place on Omnibus IV, its primary vehicle for research-and-development work in military medical efforts.

DHA chose 56 companies in 2022 for the potential 10-year, $10 billion contract vehicle that it set up to bring findings and innovations closer to medical practices for combat casualty care.

DHA is eyeing late September 2026 for the release of an on-ramp solicitation that will be set-aside for 8(a) companies, the agency said in a Monday SAM.gov notice. This timeline is later than DHA originally anticipated, but the agency added it needs more time to implement guidance stemming from the Federal Acquisition Regulation overhaul.

The agency said it has awarded 55 task orders to-date with an accumulated ceiling value of roughly $630 million since Omnibus IV opened for business.

Of those 55 orders, 36 went to small businesses and 11 were awarded to an 8(a) company. Eight orders were set-aside under the 8(a) program.

Omnibus IV’s end user base includes DHA itself, the Army Medical Research Acquisition Activity, Naval Supply Systems Command and Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences.

text:
When it’s PCS time for military personnel and their families, that means a permanent change of station is at hand and attention turns to the logistics of moving and the consuming ritual of packing and junking goods to arrive at a new duty assignment in good order.

Beyond dealing with boxes, tape and debris, there are also administrative tasks to take care of, especially relating to the government health care program known as TRICARE, which provides insurance coverage to the military community.

TRICARE moves with enrollees, but action must be taken to ensure coverage continues. According to TRICARE’s website, no changes are needed until boots hit the ground at a new assignment, but once there, it is necessary to update information in the military’s DEERS personnel system and establish relationships with new medical providers.

A Defense Health Agency initiative provides another option in the Tampa area to access TRICARE coverage during a qualifying life event like a move.

The TRICARE Prime Demo is a pilot program started in January that gives eligible beneficiaries a new option to receive health care.

Besides active-duty family members, retirees and their family members (not eligible for Medicare/TRICARE For Life), survivors and families of mobilized Guard/Reserve members are also eligible to participate in the program. Active-duty members of the military are not eligible to participate.

The program is run by CareSource Military & Veterans (CSMV), a managed care organization active in government-sponsored health care programs. Beneficiaries use providers in CSMV’s network instead of TRICARE’s standard regional contractors like Humana.

According to TRICARE’s website, the TRICARE Prime Demo has the same copayments, cost-shares and other out-of-pocket costs as TRICARE Prime.

Pamela Drake represents CSMV at community events and works with beneficiaries to adjust their coverage. According to her, maintaining the right coverage during a QLE can be a challenge, but it is important to take care of it before the first symptom appears.

“The biggest mistake is waiting until someone needs a doctor to start thinking about healthcare,” she wrote in an email, adding, “Eligible beneficiaries generally have 90 days from the date of that change to review their coverage and make any plan changes available to them. If no one tells you that window exists, it can be easy to miss while you’re getting settled.”

text:
Servicemembers about to deploy to a danger zone or for an extended period without their significant other will be eligible to have the cost of freezing their sperm or eggs covered by the Pentagon under a three-year pilot program.

Congress mandated the program, outlined Aug. 13 in the Federal Register and first reported by Military Times, in the FY 2025 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). MOAA has long supported the effort as part of its wide-ranging support of military families; a 2022 letter from MOAA, the Military Family Building Coalition, the National Military Family Association, and the Global SOF Foundation championed a similar proposal that would’ve offered cryopreservation to 1,000 servicemembers deploying for combat and special operations.

[READ THE LETTER]

Providing servicemembers with fertility preservation options gained increased attention during the Iraq and Afghanistan conflicts given the high number of injuries caused by improvised explosive devices (IEDs) which left many wounded servicemembers with significant challenges to family building. These challenges were brought to greater public attention through stories of couples such as Jason and Rachel Hallett and Aaron and Kat Causey, who shared their struggles.

“Military families have earned access to reproductive services, and nowhere is that more evident than for servicemembers about to go into harm’s way,” said Karen Ruedisueli, MOAA’s director of Government Relations for Health Affairs. “MOAA looks forward to working with key officials, lawmakers, and other stakeholders to continue ensuring these families receive the care and treatment options they deserve.”

The new benefit covers up to $500 per year for sperm cryopreservation and up to $10,000 a year for oocyte cryopreservation, according to the Federal Register. To qualify, participants must:

Have orders that will allow them to receive hazardous duty pay.

Are expected by the secretary of war to receive such orders within 120 days.

Have orders that will separate them “from a spouse, domestic partner, or dating partner” for at least 180 days.

Putting Families First

MOAA’s ongoing work on behalf of military and veteran families has included supporting a range of reproduction- and fertility-related programs, such as:

A five-year pilot program allowing pregnancy to be treated as a qualifying life event for TRICARE Select enrollment, which would give growing military families more treatment options and help limit access challenges. The Improving Access to Prenatal Care for Military Families Act is included in the House version of the FY 2027 NDAA.

Efforts via the NDAA and on other legislative fronts to require TRICARE coverage of assisted reproductive technology, including in vitro fertilization (IVF) for active duty servicemembers and their families. The change would align TRICARE policy with that of plans that cover members of Congress and their staff which already approve IVF care.

The bipartisan Warrior Infertility Act, which would make infertility a presumptive condition tied to toxic exposure.

text:
Inflation figures released last week will be the first of three monthly numbers used to calculate next year’s cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for military retirees, Social Security and VA disability recipients, and other federal beneficiaries – and they could point to a smaller-than-anticipated increase.

The Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) for July was 3.1% higher than the yearly baseline, according to figures released Aug. 12. That’s the same percentage as June, and it’s down half a percentage point from May’s 3.6% – the biggest figure of the fiscal year.

[SEE THE CHART: MOAA’s COLA Watch]

A key projection released after the Aug. 12 data went public predicts a 3.6% COLA, down 0.2 percentage points from the previous month’s projection. That would be the largest adjustment since the 8.7% boost in 2023, which was driven by post-COVID inflation.

Longer-term predictions by the Congressional Budget Office released in February as part of a wide-ranging economic outlook point to smaller increases in the coming years, with COLA averaging 2.3% from 2029 to 2036.

The average of CPI-W figures from July, August, and September are used to set the new COLA. Retirees will know the adjustment after the September figures are released in mid-October.

Why It Matters

Inflation-based adjustments to military retirement pay are necessary to maintain the value of this service-earned benefit. And while there has been little legislative movement in recent years to adjust the COLA mechanism, that hasn’t always been the case:

Total Elimination: The president’s FY 1987 budget proposed eliminating military retiree COLA. Thanks in part to advocacy from MOAA (then The Retired Officers Association, or TROA) and fellow stakeholders, Congress passed a budget that restored retiree COLAs into the 1990s.

Delays: Early 1980s legislation delayed COLA effective dates by a month for three straight fiscal years (1983-85).

Deferments and Reductions: A 2010 proposal from the National Commission on Fiscal Responsibility and Reform suggested deferring military retiree COLA until age 62, and a 2013 continuing resolution reduced COLA for military retirees under age 62 by 1%. MOAA and fellow members of The Military Coalition were active in successfully combating these efforts.

text:
Submitted by the Aiken (S.C.) Chapter

To celebrate National Women Veterans Day, the Aiken (S.C.) Chapter held its inaugural Sisters in Service luncheon on June 12.

Organized by Col. Lynda Mann, USA (Ret), chapter first vice president, and her committee, the event honored women veterans from all services, ranks, and eras. Mann founded Sisters in Service while living in Washington, D.C., and wanted to replicate the event in Aiken. The audience of 75 included women veterans, female Junior ROTC cadets, and Aiken residents.

Women Veterans Day commemorates the anniversary of the day President Harry S. Truman signed into law the Women’s Armed Services Integration Act on June 12, 1948. Prior to that, only women nurses could serve in the regular and reserve forces during peacetime. The first Women Veterans Day was celebrated June 12, 2008, and is commemorated in several states, including South Carolina.

[RELATED: Inside the Military Women’s Memorial]

Gen. Jacqueline Van Ovost, USAF (Ret), who served as 14th commander of U.S. Transportation Command, was the event’s keynote speaker.

Attendees received a bookmark inscribed with “Let Freedom Ring,” each individually handcrafted by Barbara Fusia, whose mother was in the first Women’s Army Auxiliary Corps class during World War II. Former Army Capt. Linda Caldwell, past president of MOAA’s South Carolina Council of Chapters, worked with a graphic arts class at the University of South Carolina Aiken to develop a Sisters in Service logo.

South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster issued a proclamation for Women Veterans Day, which was presented to Mann and the Sisters in Service committee by state Reps. Bill Taylor and Charlie Hartz.

Plans are underway to make this an annual event.

text:
The Council of Autism Service Providers (CASP) has elected Amego President and CEO John Randall as chair of its board of directors and Aspire Behavior Solutions owner and COO Amy Legan as a new board member, adding two experienced autism services executives to the nonprofit trade association’s leadership.

Randall has led Amego since 2008 and has worked in human services and education since 1988. During his tenure as president and CEO, Amego expanded its services to include applied behavior analysis, or ABA, for the treatment of autism.

His experience also includes leadership roles across professional organizations involved in behavioral health and developmental disability services. Randall previously served as president of the Massachusetts Association for Applied Behavior Analysis and currently serves on the board of the Massachusetts Association of Developmental Disabilities Providers.

As CASP board chair, Randall will help lead an organization representing more than 475 autism service provider organizations across all 50 states and multiple countries. The role comes as providers navigate operational issues ranging from workforce capacity and reimbursement to regulatory requirements, clinical standards and access to services.

“It’s a privilege to work with my colleagues to bring providers closer together on the issues that matter most,” Randall said. “I’m confident that, together, we can make meaningful progress.”

Legan brings a small-provider operating perspective to the CASP board. She founded Aspire Behavior Solutions in Alaska in 2018 and serves as the organization’s owner and COO.

Her work with CASP has included co-leading the association’s small business and TRICARE special interest groups. Those groups bring providers together around operational challenges affecting ABA organizations, including access to care and issues facing smaller businesses.

text:
This is a notice of intent to award a sole-source contract modification and is not a request for competitive quotes. A sole source justification in accordance with FAR Part 6 is being processed for this requirement and will be posted when the approval process is accomplished.

The MHS GENESIS program recently underwent a strategic acquisition realignment driven by updated executive management priorities, federal efficiency initiatives, and joint DoD/VA healthcare data exchange goals. This shift focused the program on performance-based outcomes, agile business system integration, and rapid scaling capabilities. Consequently, the timeframe to complete pre-solicitation, solicitation, source selection, and award was compressed from 36 months down to a 12-to-18-month window.

When the Swingtide, Inc. contract was originally awarded, the exact number of required follow-on contract actions was unknown, with a baseline goal to complete all transition actions by July 2025. However, due to the complexity of establishing the multi-vendor paradigm, the formal acquisition strategy and master schedule were not finalized and approved until April 2026. This left insufficient time to execute the strategy under a traditional acquisition lifecycle.

To resolve this schedule constraint and comply with Executive Order 14222, the approved strategy shifts the DHMSM PMO from its legacy single Lead Systems Integrator model to a modular, multi-contractor framework. This strategy maximizes competitive procurement by contracting directly with original commercial solution providers for core software capabilities, while competitively sourcing all remaining integration and support services.

Operationalizing this modular framework requires the Government to concurrently plan, draft, and execute ten (10) distinct contracting actions within a compressed 12-to-15-month schedule. This complex effort involves negotiating and awarding five (5) sole-source contract vehicles for proprietary solutions, alongside competing up to five (5) new contracts for services.

This contract modification to extend the period of performance (PoP) of the contract by an additional 14 months is critical to providing the uninterrupted market intelligence and source selection advisory support required to orchestrate these concurrent awards on schedule and without disruption to critical federal healthcare operations.

The services falling under this J&A include:

I. Enterprise Market Intelligence & Commercial Practices Alignment

Swingtide, Inc. will leverage its specialized experience in commercial healthcare contracts to assist the Government in aligning the MHS GENESIS recompete with modern commercial practices. These advisory services include:

Outcome-Based Acquisition Design: Shifting procurement focus from prescriptive methods to desired clinical and operational outcomes.

Commercial Flexibility & Innovation: Structuring solicitations to encourage innovative EHR capabilities, even when deviating from original specifications.

Solicitation Simplification: Constructing plain-language structures to lower barriers of entry for high-quality commercial vendors.

Value & ROI Optimization: Prioritizing total value, long-term sustainability, and ROI over strict “lowest price” models.

Collaborative Vendor Engagement: Enhancing transparent, interactive dialogue with potential industry partners.

II. Transition Oversight & Coordination Support

Swingtide, Inc. will provide enterprise-level management and oversight to orchestrate decomposing the legacy bundled contract into multiple modular awards:

Process Orchestration: Driving the development and source selection process from initiation to completion.

Interdependency & Integration Management: Serving as the central coordination node across all DHMSM® PMO stakeholders.

Schedule & Risk Tracking: Implementing a system to track milestones, manage resource schedules, and mitigate risks.

III. Source Selection & Award Execution

Swingtide, Inc. will deliver direct support to the Government during the critical evaluation and award phases:

Evaluation Plan Support: Assisting in drafting a comprehensive source selection plan.

Proposal Evaluation Advisory: Providing expert technical and commercial guidance during evaluations to ensure compliance.

Solicitation Q&A Management: Collecting, consolidating, and anonymizing vendor questions, and drafting proposed responses for Government approval.

Award Justification Documentation: Drafting comprehensive risk assessments and supporting the development of well-documented source selection decisions.

text:
Are you looking for other ways to get your prescriptions that better fit your pharmacy needs? You’re in luck! When it comes to your prescriptions, the TRICARE Pharmacy Program gives you several options on how to fill them. Before filling your prescriptions, you can check the TRICARE Formulary to see if your prescription is covered.

“TRICARE beneficiaries can fill prescriptions a number of different ways,” said Marcy Opstal, Senior Program Analyst, Pharmacy Benefit Integration Branch, Pharmacy Operations Division, at the Defense Health Agency. “These options give you flexibility and allow you to pick what works best for you.”

The TRICARE Pharmacy Program contractor, Express Scripts, administers the TRICARE pharmacy benefit and offers tools to help you manage your medications. Here’s a rundown of your TRICARE pharmacy choices.

Pick the best pharmacy option for you

TRICARE offers four ways to fill your prescriptions. Each option has different costs and advantages.

Military pharmacies

At military pharmacies, you can get up to a 90-day supply of most medications at no cost. Most military pharmacies take prescriptions from both civilian and military providers. You don’t need to be enrolled at a military hospital or clinic to use its pharmacy, as described in the TRICARE Pharmacy Program Handbook.

Military pharmacies only carry medications that are on the TRICARE formulary. Call your nearest military pharmacy to see if they have your medication. Visit Military Pharmacy to find one near you.

Home delivery

TRICARE Pharmacy Home Delivery is generally the least expensive way to fill prescriptions after military pharmacies. Active duty service members pay nothing for home delivery. All others pay a copayment. Home delivery offers up to a 90-day supply of most drugs for lower copayments than a 30-day supply at a TRICARE network pharmacy.

Home delivery is a good option for medications you take routinely. Shipping is free, and you can order refills online, by phone, or by mail. You’ll get updates about your order and reminders when it’s time to refill.

TRICARE Pharmacy Home Delivery will ship to any address in the U.S. or U.S. territories, including APO/FPO addresses. Medications requiring refrigerated packaging or that have pressurized dispensing devices won’t ship to APO/FPO/DPO addresses.

Important: Home delivery isn’t available in Germany, Norway, or Saudi Arabia. If you have other health insurance with drug coverage, you can’t use home delivery, unless:

Express Scripts also manages your OHI’s pharmacy home delivery.

Your OHI doesn’t cover pharmacy benefits.

Your medication isn’t covered by your OHI.

You met your OHI’s benefit cap.

Network pharmacies

You can fill up to a 30-day supply of prescriptions at TRICARE’s network of retail pharmacies, too. Use the Find a Pharmacy Tool to find a network pharmacy nearby. Check out Pharmacy Costs to compare what you’ll pay at different pharmacies.

Note: Network pharmacies are only available in the U.S. and certain U.S. territories (Guam, the Northern Islands, Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands).

Non-network pharmacies

You’re also able to fill your prescription at a non-network pharmacy. If you use a non-network pharmacy, you’ll pay the full price for your prescription drugs up front and file for reimbursement on your own. The reimbursement amount has cost-sharing as well.

Note: Reimbursements are subject to deductibles or non-network cost-shares and copayments.

Wherever you go, remember that you’ll pay the full cost of any non-covered drugs.

Using the Express Scripts Pharmacy Mobile app

The free Express Scripts mobile app helps you manage your prescriptions from your phone. Visit the Apple App Store or Google Play Store to download the free app today.

How you can use the app

The Express Scripts Pharmacy Mobile App makes keeping track of your prescriptions easier.

Order medications. See which prescriptions are available to refill, compare costs, and choose the medications you want delivered to your door.

Track medications. Get updates as Express Scripts fills and ships your order. You can send your medication to a temporary address if you’re deployed, moving, or on vacation. If you move, your order will go to your new address.

Request refills. See what prescriptions are ready to refill and where you can save money. You can transfer a prescription from another pharmacy to TRICARE Pharmacy Home Delivery right in the app.

Set up reminders. The app can send you reminders when it’s time to take your medications.

Pay online. Pay for prescriptions and set up automatic payments for home delivery. Active duty service members always pay nothing for up to a 90-day supply.

Set up your Express Scripts account

You’ll need an account to use the app and manage prescriptions online. Create an Express Scripts account to get started.

Get help any time

For other details about your pharmacy benefit, go to the TRICARE Pharmacy Program Handbook. You can also reach out to Express Scripts with any questions.

text:
Compassionate, Confidential Care for Those Who Serve and Their Families

Military life can place extraordinary demands on service members and their loved ones. Deployments, reintegration, frequent transitions, operational stress, trauma, and separation from family can all affect emotional well-being.

Williamsville Psychiatry provides respectful, evidence-based mental health care for active-duty service members, retirees, veterans, National Guard and Reserve members, and military families. Our goal is to make treatment accessible, personalized, and free from judgment.

Mental Health Services

Our services include:

Comprehensive psychiatric evaluations

Medication management

Individual psychotherapy

Treatment for depression and anxiety

PTSD and trauma-related care

ADHD treatment

OCD treatment

Mood disorder treatment

Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS)

Telepsychiatry for eligible patients located in New York

TRICARE Covers TMS for Major Depression

Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is an FDA-cleared, noninvasive treatment for adults with major depressive disorder. It may be appropriate when antidepressant medications have not provided adequate relief or have caused difficult side effects.

TRICARE covers outpatient TMS for adults with major depressive disorder when applicable medical necessity and authorization requirements are met. Williamsville Psychiatry can help determine eligibility, verify benefits, gather clinical documentation, and request prior authorization when required.

Coverage is determined by the patient's specific TRICARE plan, eligibility, diagnosis, treatment history, referral requirements, and authorization decision. Learn more from the official TRICARE TMS Coverage Page .

What to Expect From TMS

TMS uses focused magnetic pulses to stimulate areas of the brain involved in mood regulation. Treatment:

Does not require anesthesia

Is performed in an outpatient office

Allows most patients to resume normal activities immediately

Does not cause the systemic medication side effects associated with many antidepressants

Is administered through a structured series of treatment sessions

Every patient receives an individualized evaluation to determine whether TMS is clinically appropriate.

Care Designed Around Military Life

We recognize that service members and military families may face concerns that are different from those encountered in civilian life. Treatment is individualized around symptoms, responsibilities, family circumstances, treatment history, and personal goals.

Seeking care is a sign of strength. Early treatment can help protect health, relationships, functioning, and quality of life.

Schedule an Appointment

Williamsville Psychiatry welcomes TRICARE beneficiaries and offers timely access to psychiatric care and TMS evaluations.

Call 716-886-5493 to schedule an appointment or request a TMS eligibility review.

If you are experiencing an immediate mental health emergency, call 911, call or text 988, or go to the nearest emergency department. Service members and veterans may call 988 and press 1 to reach the Veterans Crisis Line.

TRICARE coverage and authorization are not guaranteed. Benefits must be verified for each patient, and applicable referrals, clinical criteria, and prior-authorization requirements must be satisfied.

text:
About

In 1947, Marine Corps Reserve Major Bill Hendricks was preparing for the holidays with his family in Los Angeles, CA. His wife, Diane, was an altruistic mother with nimble fingers and a knack for handcrafting. She handmade a few dolls during the holidays that year and asked her husband to donate them to an agency that supported children in need. The agency he sought didn’t exist - not yet.

Hendricks returned to his wife with the disheartening news, but instead of fretting, she inspired him to “start one!” He proceeded to round up the Marines in his unit to create a way to donate the dolls to children in need. They collected and distributed 5,000 toys that year.

Seeing the impact it created, the Commandant of the Marine Corps, Gen Clifton B. Cates, directed all Reserve units to implement a Toys for Tots campaign in 1948, making the Program national.

Hendricks’ civilian job was as Director of Public Relations for Warner Brothers Studios, he used his connections to support the Program to expand its reach. As a favor to his friend Bill, Walt Disney created the first Toys for Tots poster that was adopted as the official logo.

More than seventy-five years later, Toys for Tots now distributes an average of 18 million toys and books to over 7 million less fortunate children across the Nation.
